source.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
source.authors: Aaditya K. Singh; Ted Moskovitz; Felix Hill; Stephanie C. Y. Chan; Andrew M. Saxe

record.tranche_reason: The study trains two-layer attention-only transformers and measures induction behavior and task performance, while refining the phase-change account with causal clamps that identify multiple interacting subcircuits.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own induction-strength, loss, accuracy, ablation, and clamping outcomes. Values used only to motivate or select clamp implementations are not recorded as results. The paper also cites findings from prior studies; those cited results are not recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study trains 2-layer attention-only transformers on a synthetic few-shot (Omniglot exemplar-label) task and reports its own results on induction-circuit mechanism (V1), phase-change timing (V2), data dependence (V5) and seed reproducibility (V4, training runs only). Its causal clamps argue that the phase change comes from three interacting, smoothly learned subcircuits, which bears on V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that induction heads act additively and redundantly, and that extra heads speed up learning without being necessary. PT-to-induction wiring is many-to-many, with notable V-composition. Three smoothly evolving subcircuits (PT attend/copy, QK match, label copy) interact to produce the phase change, and class and label counts delay formation through different subcircuits.
record.recipe_differences: Uses two-layer attention-only transformers and an induction-strength measure in the spirit of prior induction-head work, but trains on a synthetic Omniglot few-shot classification task rather than natural-language text. Adds causal activation clamps throughout training to isolate subcircuits.
record.method_sensitivity: Class count and label count shift phase-change timing through different subcircuits; initialization seeds show mostly similar results, with some variation in the label-scaling result. Different activation clamps change the loss dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: When trained alone with the others ablated, every Layer 2 head can learn the task, but its phase change is delayed (Fig 4b). Heads add their effects and are redundant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple induction heads form redundantly and additively, and the extra heads speed up formation.

fits_no_version.finding: With 2 labels, a clamped anti-induction head (strength -1) gives an alternative ICL circuit (Fig 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alternative match-and-copy circuits are learnable depending on the label count.

record.problems: The experiments use a small, two-layer attention-only model and one synthetic task, rather than large natural-language models. Most reported dynamics are described from plotted curves without uncertainty estimates. Some supplementary per-head results are presented graphically or qualitatively.
record.rows_left_out: Supplementary per-head error analyses concerning the residual-head hypothesis (Appendix H, Tables 2-3 and Figures 16-17) are not separately recorded because they do not directly test the listed claim versions beyond the head-performance and redundancy outcomes already captured. Figure-only individual-head curve values are also not transcribed where the text gives no corresponding numerical value.

untested.parts: The loss bump and in-context learning measured as loss falling with token index. Training loss is on the last token only.
All of it: no large models and no token-index ICL.
Model families, sizes, architectures and natural-language modalities. Only seeds within one small setup are tested.
All of it: the task is exemplar-label match-and-copy, not few-shot task learning distinct from copying.
Data properties other than class and label counts, and whether ICL persists.

missing.what: Pattern-preserving ablation of all Layer 1 heads drops accuracy to 55%; value-preserving ablation drops it to 11%.
Single-Layer-2-head training runs each learn the task, with shifted phase-change timing.
Layer 1 to output ablation costs 0.01% at the end of training, but Layer 1 contributes before the phase change (likely skip-trigrams).
Clamping all Layer 1 heads to previous-token patterns severely slows learning.

record.verdict_notes: Removed the record's V6 'challenges' label: the task is literal match-and-copy, so it does not separate task learning from copying. Removed V2 'limits_scope' from the clamp rows: those runs are artificial interventions and now link only to V7. Added a weak V4 verdict from seed reproducibility. The model uses LayerNorm and RoPE, and the inputs are ResNet image embeddings.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests an analogous exemplar-label match-and-copy circuit in a synthetic few-shot task, not the full range of repeated-token sequences or transformer sizes.
The study tests phase-change timing in its synthetic task, but does not establish that the loss curve has a bump; it does not test large natural-language transformers.
The study does not test whether induction heads account for most token-index ICL in large transformers.
The study does not compare model families, substantially different sizes, architectures, or modalities.
The data variations tested are number of classes and number of labels in one synthetic task; other data properties and training setups are not tested.
The study tests task performance in its synthetic few-shot classification setting, not few-shot task learning across natural-language tasks or large models.
The study identifies three interacting subcircuits in its chosen setup; it does not establish that all induction-head formation in other settings has the same decomposition.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Measured Layer 2 induction strength as attention to the correct in-context label minus attention to the incorrect label.
rows.value: All Layer 2 heads show some induction-like behavior; Head 3 is strongest and emerges first.
rows.note: The measure concerns matching the query exemplar to the earlier exemplar and attending to its associated label in the synthetic task.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Tracked training loss and task accuracy during training.
rows.baseline: Initial/plateau performance: approximately 50% accuracy and loss of log 2.
rows.value: After a plateau, loss changes suddenly to near 0 and task accuracy reaches 99.99%; the paper says the change corresponds to induction-circuit formation. It also reports strong generalization to held-out exemplars and label pairs.
rows.note: The reported curve is a plateau followed by a sudden loss reduction; the text does not describe a bump in loss.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Ablated one Layer 2 head at a time and measured task accuracy.

conditions.value: each Layer 2 head, one at a time

rows.value: Ablating a single head causes virtually no decrease in task performance, except ablating Head 3, which causes a 1% decrease.
rows.note: The paper attributes the small individual-ablation effects to redundancy among heads.
rows.check: Single-head knockouts cannot show the mechanism because heads are redundant. The paper calls this ablation uninformative. It also does not bear on V6: the task is literal label match-and-copy, not few-shot task learning.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Ablated all Layer 2 heads except one, evaluating each remaining head's task performance.

conditions.value: one Layer 2 head at a time

rows.baseline: Chance level is 20%; a simple context-copying strategy is 50%.
rows.value: Head 3 alone achieves 98% accuracy; the paper states that other single heads also achieve strong performance.
rows.note: This synthetic task is a two-way, one-shot classification task; the result shows that an induction head can carry high task performance in this setting.
rows.check: Head 3 alone reaches 98%, showing a single induction head carries the match-and-copy task. Unlink from V6, since the task is copying, not the task learning V6 distinguishes.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Ablated Layer 1 previous-token heads while preserving Layer 2 attention patterns.
rows.note: The authors interpret these heads as previous-token heads that primarily compose with the match subcircuit.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Ablated Layer 1 previous-token heads while preserving Layer 2 value vectors.
rows.note: This ablation leaves substantial task performance, while the authors use the result to distinguish previous-token heads' role in matching from other Layer 1 heads' value composition.
rows.check: Ablating PT heads while preserving values drops accuracy to 69.87% (from ~99.99%). This shows PT heads feed the match step, but the drop is incomplete.

rows.subject: 2-layer attention-only transformer (default setting)
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 8 heads per layer, model dimension 64
rows.operation_detail: Ablated other Layer 1 heads while preserving Layer 2 attention patterns.
rows.note: The paper identifies these other Layer 1 heads as primarily participating in value composition.
rows.check: This row shows an addition to V1: non-PT Layer 1 heads feed Layer 2 values (V-composition), and removing them drops accuracy to 34.27%. The mechanism is more than PT-head K-composition alone.

rows.measure: Reproduction of reported induction and subcircuit results
rows.value: The authors report little to no difference when the data-ordering seed is varied; main subcircuit results hold across initialization seeds. The scaling result reproduces across most seeds, though in some standard-training runs learning with 15 labels is as quick as with 10.
rows.note: The paper describes these replications qualitatively and points to notebooks for further details.
rows.check: Induction circuits form across 5 initialization seeds (bears on V4, training runs only). The label-count delay is not reproduced in every seed: 15 labels is sometimes as fast as 10.

relationships.reason: Layer 2 heads become induction-like (r1), and a single head solves the task (r4). PT heads feed the match step (r5, r6, r8), and the L1H2→L2H3 path alone gives 90% (r9).
relationships.display_finding: Layer-2 heads became induction-like and a single head solved the task; previous-token heads fed matching, with the L1H2→L2H3 path alone achieving 90% accuracy.

source_check.reason: r1, r4–r6, r8 and r9 support previous-token composition and induction-based matching and copying. The 90% result in r9 specifically preserves Layer-2 values.

relationships.reason: Copying relies on V-composition from non-PT Layer 1 heads, dropping to 34.27% when they are removed (r7). PT-to-induction wiring is many-to-many rather than one PT head per induction head (r9).
relationships.display_finding: Removing layer-1 heads without previous-token attention reduced copying accuracy to 34.27%, and previous-token heads connected to induction heads through many-to-many wiring.

relation.reason: The study reports its own induction measurements, causal ablations, training interventions, and data-scaling experiments.

tranche.reason: Causal interventions refine the account of induction-circuit formation by identifying three interacting subcircuits, additional value composition, and many-to-many wiring.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately summarized, but subcircuit interaction is presented as an explanation that may account for the phase change. Section 4.2 calls durations iterations, whereas the associated plots use sequences seen; preserve this source terminology discrepancy.

statements.correction: L1H2→L2H3 accuracy: 90% with Layer-2 values preserved from the unablated forward pass; Appendix E, Figure 11b.
statements.problem: The 90% path result omits value preservation; it does not demonstrate that the isolated pair performs the entire computation unaided.

statements.correction: Appendix I: five initialization seeds; strongest-head performance and subcircuit findings reproduce; scaling reproduces across most seeds, with exceptions between 10 and 15 labels. Little to no difference is reported for variation of the data-ordering seed.
statements.problem: The statement attributes little to no difference to initialization seeds; the paper makes that statement about the data-ordering seed.

statements.correction: Section 4.2 uses Layer-2 Head 3 as the sole active induction head. Clamps intervene on attention patterns, Layer-2 inputs, or output logits depending on the operation. Steps 1–2 clamped: approximately 7.5e4 iterations versus 2e5 unclamped.
statements.problem: The clamp summary omits the single-active-Layer-2-head setting and describes all interventions as attention clamps, although some replace residual inputs or output logits.

statements.correction: Section 4.2 isolates Layer-2 Head 3. Match clamping fixes its attention pattern; copy clamping substitutes its attention logits for output logits. Three interacting subcircuits explain one abrupt transition in unclamped training.
statements.problem: The clamp summary omits the restriction to Layer-2 Head 3 and describes interventions beyond attention patterns as attention clamping.
